sources.title: GHSA Critical (npm:ruflo): ruflo MCP bridge allows unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose deployments

incidents.title: ruflo MCP bridge: unauthenticated RCE in default Docker Compose deployments (CVE-2026-59726)
incidents.evidenceQuote: The MCP bridge shipping in ruflo/docker-compose.yml exposed POST /mcp with no authentication.
incidents.attackSurface: Local AI dev tools / MCP server
incidents.tldrRootCause: ruflo's default Docker Compose setup exposed an unauthenticated MCP endpoint and MongoDB on all network interfaces, allowing remote command execution.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A network attacker could call terminal_execute through POST /mcp, get a shell in the bridge container and read every provider API key from its environment. They could also plant poisoned patterns in the AgentDB store. The advisory does not say this has been exploited.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you run ruflo from its docker-compose.yml: look for the ruflo npm package and containers listening on ports 3001 and 27017.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: If you started ruflo with the default compose file on a laptop or cloud VM, anyone who can reach ports 3001 or 27017 on that host could run commands and take your AI provider keys.
lockItDown: Check whether ruflo is installed or running in Docker. If so, confirm ports 3001 and 27017 are bound to loopback only, and redeploy from the patched release.

If an instance was ever network-reachable, rotate the OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter and Anthropic keys it held and audit the AgentDB pattern store. The advisory says patching alone does not undo poisoning.
incidents.roleAngle: A clear example of AI tooling shipping insecure defaults: no authentication, all-interface binds, and provider keys in the container environment.

incidents.title: 1Password breach: compromised employee GitHub account used to push malicious backend code
incidents.evidenceQuote: A hacker used a compromised employee GitHub account to push malicious code and steal customer records
incidents.tldrRootCause: An attacker took over an employee's corporate GitHub account and used it to deploy malicious code to backend services.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The compromised account was used to push code that reached 1Password's backend and stole customer records and internal source code; vaults were reportedly not accessed. How the GitHub account itself was compromised is not stated in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the technique applies: if one GitHub account can push code that deploys to production without a second review, you have the same exposure.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A stolen GitHub session, token or sign-in for you or a colleague could be used to push code that your pipelines deploy into cloud environments.
lockItDown: In GitHub Settings, review Sessions, SSH and GPG keys, and Personal access tokens; revoke anything you do not recognise or no longer use.
On repositories that deploy to production, check branch protection or rulesets require pull request approval from a second person and do not allow bypass.
incidents.roleAngle: A single developer identity was enough to reach production data; it is worth checking whether your deploy path has the same gap.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension

incidents.title: Remus infostealer reads Gmail through a fake Google Sheets Chrome extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: An infostealer already on the machine uses a malicious Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets to read Gmail messages.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The Remus infostealer steals mail through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, which its operators marketed as a Gmail zero-day. How Remus first reaches the endpoint is not stated in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if an infostealer lands on your Mac or Windows laptop; look for a Google Sheets extension in Chrome that you did not install.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: If Remus runs on your laptop, the extension works inside your signed-in browser session and can read mail, including password resets and security alerts for your cloud and GitHub accounts.
lockItDown: Open chrome://extensions in every Chrome profile and remove any Google Sheets or other Google-branded extension you did not install yourself, especially ones not installed from the Chrome Web Store.
In Google Workspace admin (Chrome browser extension settings), check whether extension installs are limited to an allowlist rather than open to users.
incidents.roleAngle: Mail read from inside the browser session sidesteps sign-in protections, so extension control is part of identity security.

incidents.title: SAP confirms incident; stolen employee GitHub tokens reportedly used on source code
incidents.evidenceQuote: hackers reportedly used stolen employee tokens to copy and alter source code
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers reportedly used stolen employee GitHub tokens to copy and alter SAP source code.
incidents.realisticRootCause: SAP detected suspicious activity on GitHub and confirmed an incident in its development infrastructure. The token theft is reported rather than confirmed by SAP, and how the tokens were stolen is not stated.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes; any long-lived GitHub token on a laptop or in a config file gives the same access if it is stolen.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A personal access token or SSH key taken from your machine or a leaked file lets an attacker clone and push to every repository that token can reach, without going through SSO sign-in.
lockItDown: In GitHub Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens, delete unused tokens and check that the rest have an expiry date and narrow repository scope.

In your GitHub organisation settings, review the personal access token policy (restrict classic tokens, require approval for fine-grained ones) and scan the audit log for unfamiliar clone or push activity.
incidents.roleAngle: Developer tokens are standing credentials that bypass SSO, so their inventory and expiry deserve the same attention as cloud access keys.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook

incidents.title: SYS01 infostealer enrols browsers in fake management to force a mail-stealing extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management to force the installation of an extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: Malware delivered through Meta ads puts the browser under enterprise-style management and force-installs a data-stealing extension.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A new SYS01 infostealer version, delivered through Meta ads, enrols the browser into enterprise-style management. That lets it force-install an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if someone on a Mac or Windows laptop runs a download from a malicious Meta ad; the browser then shows as managed by an unknown party.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A lure download run on a laptop could put your browser under attacker-set policy and install an extension that reads webmail, and with it password-reset and SSO-related mail.
lockItDown: Open chrome://management and edge://management. An unmanaged browser should say so, and a work browser should name only your own organisation.
Open chrome://policy or edge://policy and look for force-installed extension entries (ExtensionInstallForcelist) you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: Browser policy is being used as a persistence mechanism, so unexpected management enrolment is worth treating as a detection signal.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Microsoft Fixes Azure API Management Classic Flaw as Actor Targets Customer Secrets

incidents.title: Microsoft fixes Azure API Management Classic flaw; actor hunting customer secrets
incidents.evidenceQuote: Microsoft Fixes Azure API Management Classic Flaw as Actor Targets Customer Secrets
incidents.tldrRootCause: A flaw in Azure API Management Classic was used by an unknown actor to look for access tokens, secrets and named values.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Norway's NSM says a vulnerability in Azure APIM affected multiple businesses and that an unknown actor has been searching APIM for access tokens, secrets and named values. The excerpt does not give the exact mechanism and says parts are still uncertain.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if any of your Azure subscriptions has an API Management instance, especially a classic one with secrets stored as named values.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Secrets stored in APIM named values, or tokens handled by APIM, could be read by the actor and reused against backend APIs and cloud resources.
lockItDown: In the Azure portal, list API Management services across your subscriptions and note any classic instances; check Microsoft's advisory for whether they were affected.
On each instance, open Named values: rotate any secrets stored there, and consider moving them to Key Vault references.
incidents.roleAngle: A managed-service flaw exposed customer-held secrets; it is worth knowing which secrets sit in API gateways rather than in a vault.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware

incidents.title: PolinRider campaign plants malware in over 7,600 GitHub repositories of real developers
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not disclosed how the developers' repositories were taken over; attackers planted a Python loader in some of them.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Not disclosed in the excerpt. What is known is that over 7,600 repositories belonging to real developers were compromised, some with a Python loader that fetches next-stage payloads, with activity possibly dating back to February 2025.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, in two ways: your own GitHub repos could be tampered with, or you could clone and run a poisoned repo.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Cloning and running code from an affected repository could execute the loader on your laptop, and a compromised developer account or machine could see its own repos poisoned in turn.
lockItDown: In GitHub, open Settings > Security log and your repos' recent commit history; look for commits or force-pushes you did not make.
Before running a freshly cloned third-party repo, review its build, setup and config scripts for obfuscated or unexpected Python loader code.
incidents.roleAngle: The repositories belong to real developer accounts, not throwaways, so account or repository reputation is not a reliable trust signal.

sources.title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

incidents.title: NFS2ROOT: 12-year-old Linux kernel NFS server flaw allows remote root (CVE-2026-99362)
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
incidents.attackSurface: Linux kernel NFS server on cloud hosts / K8s nodes
incidents.tldrRootCause: A flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server lets a remote attacker gain root; the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The teaser describes a critical, 12-year-old vulnerability in the Linux kernel's NFS server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, that gives remote attackers root. Affected kernel versions, preconditions and patch status are not in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if any of your Linux VMs or Kubernetes nodes run the kernel NFS server and the NFS port is reachable by untrusted networks.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A Linux instance or node in your cloud environment that exports NFS shares could be attacked over the network by anyone who can reach its NFS service.
lockItDown: Inventory Linux VMs and K8s nodes that run the kernel NFS server (self-hosted NFS exports or in-cluster NFS provisioners) and track the distro kernel fix for CVE-2026-99362.
Review security groups, firewall rules and NetworkPolicies so the NFS port (2049) on those hosts is only reachable from the specific clients that need it.
incidents.roleAngle: The teaser shows exposure only for hosts acting as an NFS server, so scoping that inventory is the first step.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Com-Affiliated Hackers Hijack Cloud Accounts via Vishing for Data Theft and Extortion

incidents.title: Com-affiliated actors use vishing to hijack cloud accounts for data theft and extortion
incidents.evidenceQuote: Com-Affiliated Hackers Hijack Cloud Accounts via Vishing for Data Theft and Extortion
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers used voice phishing (vishing) calls to take over cloud accounts, then stole data and attempted extortion.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Unit 42 reports numerous waves of vishing by Com-affiliated actors since August 2026 that led to cloud account hijacking, data theft and extortion attempts. The excerpt does not say who was called or how the calls were turned into account access.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the technique targets the SSO and cloud accounts you rely on; it depends on how your help desk and staff handle phone requests.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A caller persuading you, a colleague or your help desk to hand over or reset sign-in details could give an attacker an SSO session that reaches your cloud consoles and GitHub.
lockItDown: In your identity provider's audit log, review recent MFA method registrations and password or MFA resets, especially for cloud admin accounts, and confirm each was expected.
Check how your help desk verifies a caller's identity before resetting a password or MFA, and whether that check could be passed by phone alone.
incidents.roleAngle: Phone-based social engineering remains a working route into cloud tenants; reset and enrolment procedures are the control to test.

sources.name: Google Project Zero
sources.title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?

incidents.title: Project Zero: .NET loading quirk bypasses VirtualBox hardening and Windows code integrity
incidents.evidenceQuote: permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process
incidents.tldrRootCause: A .NET Framework assembly-loading behaviour lets a local attacker load untrusted code into VirtualBox's protected process on Windows.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-87268 combines .NET's ability to load assemblies from memory with VirtualBox's DLL loader hooks to defeat process hardening, which guards access to its kernel driver. The same behaviour bypassed Windows code integrity. This is researcher-reported, and the evidence mentions no attacks in the wild.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if an attacker already runs code on your Windows laptop; it matters most if Oracle VirtualBox is installed there.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Malware or a local user already on a Windows laptop with VirtualBox could use the bypass to reach the VirtualBox kernel driver and possibly escalate privileges.
lockItDown: On Windows laptops, check Settings > Apps > Installed apps for Oracle VirtualBox; update it to the latest release, or uninstall it if unused. The fixed version is not given in the evidence.
Check Settings > Windows Update and confirm the latest cumulative update is installed.

sources.name: Huntress Threat Research
sources.title: Three Attacks, Zero Exploits in Microsoft 365

incidents.title: Huntress: three Microsoft 365 compromises that used no exploits, only user actions
incidents.tldrRootCause: Likely social engineering: the teaser says ordinary user actions led to full Microsoft 365 compromise, with no exploits involved.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The teaser does not name the three techniques. The reporting suggests they depend on users being tricked into ordinary actions such as signing in or approving something, rather than on a software flaw.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if you use Microsoft 365 or Entra ID for SSO; these attacks rely on user actions rather than unpatched software.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A user in your tenant who performs a routine-looking sign-in or approval at an attacker's prompt could hand over mailbox or tenant access through SSO.
lockItDown: In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise applications > Consent and permissions and confirm users cannot consent to apps from unverified publishers.
Review Enterprise applications for recently added apps with mail or file permissions that you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: A reminder that identity compromise in Microsoft 365 often needs no vulnerability; read the full post for the three specific techniques.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Okta Links ShinyHunters-Associated Vishing Group to New INCEPTION Data Leak Site

incidents.title: Okta ties ShinyHunters-linked vishing cluster to new INCEPTION data leak site
incidents.evidenceQuote: use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers phone targets and talk them into entering credentials on phishing pages and approving prompts.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Okta's cluster O-UNC-053 uses voice phishing to get targets to enter SSO credentials on phishing pages and approve something further (the excerpt cuts off). The group may now be operating a leak site under the name INCEPTION.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if your SSO sign-in can be completed with a password plus a push or code that a caller could talk you into approving.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A caller posing as IT support directs you to a look-alike SSO page; your credentials and approval give them a session into the SaaS and cloud apps behind SSO.
lockItDown: In your identity provider's authentication policies, check whether admin and cloud console apps require a phishing-resistant factor (FIDO2/passkey) rather than push or OTP.
Review your own SSO account's enrolled authenticators and recent sign-ins for devices or sessions you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: Vishing-led SSO compromise continues under a new brand, so the control that matters is phishing-resistant authentication, not tracking the group name.

sources.name: Microsoft Security Blog (Threat Intelligence)
sources.title: What defenders need to know about ARTEX, the agentic AI framework threat actors abuse

incidents.title: Microsoft: ARTEX AI pentest framework abused by state and criminal actors
incidents.evidenceQuote: abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation
incidents.tldrRootCause: Tooling research, not one breach: actors use ARTEX to automate secret hunting in public repos, scanning and credential attacks.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Microsoft says several named state-sponsored and financially motivated groups have integrated ARTEX to speed up network reconnaissance, credential attacks and web application exploitation. The attacker sets scope and targets, and AI agents plan the steps, run the tools and report back.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if a secret sits in a public GitHub repo or an internet-facing cloud service is unpatched; these tools find such gaps faster.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An automated agent finds a cloud key or token committed to a public repository, or an exposed web application in your cloud estate, and uses it for access.
lockItDown: In GitHub organisation settings under Code security, confirm secret scanning and push protection are enabled for all repositories, and clear any open secret scanning alerts.
List which of your repositories are public and confirm none hold cloud keys, tokens or kubeconfig files, including in commit history.
incidents.roleAngle: The techniques are unchanged, but the time between a secret leaking or a service being exposed and its abuse keeps shrinking.

sources.name: Huntress Threat Research
sources.title: A Buffet of ClickFix: Lures, Infrastructure & Payloads

incidents.title: Huntress recap: ClickFix lures, fake verification pages and payloads
incidents.evidenceQuote: convincing ClickFix lures, the infrastructure behind fake verification pages, varied payloads, and how to stop the paste
incidents.tldrRootCause: Technique recap, not one breach: ClickFix uses fake verification pages to get users to paste and run a command themselves.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The teaser describes a webinar recap covering ClickFix lures, the hosting behind fake verification pages and the range of payloads delivered. It names no specific victim or malware family.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes: anyone on a Windows or Mac laptop can meet a fake verification page that asks them to paste a command.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A browser page posing as a verification step asks you to paste a command into the Run dialog or a terminal, and the command installs malware that can steal sessions and cloud credentials.
lockItDown: On Windows, check the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU for Run-dialog commands you do not recognise.
For managed Windows laptops, check whether the Group Policy setting 'Remove Run menu from Start Menu' is applied to users who do not need the Run dialog.
incidents.roleAngle: ClickFix bypasses mail and download controls because the user runs the command; the realistic controls are paste and execution restrictions and user awareness.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins

incidents.title: 'GoodGuys' phishing uses fake paid expert interviews to steal Google and Okta logins
incidents.evidenceQuote: to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars
incidents.tldrRootCause: Phishing invitations to fake paid expert interviews and webinars lead victims to hand over corporate Google and Okta credentials.
incidents.realisticRootCause: An ongoing campaign impersonates brands including Google, Nvidia, Accenture and SpaceX and offers paid expert interviews as the lure. The teaser does not say whether the pages also capture MFA codes or session tokens.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes: security professionals are plausible targets for paid expert interview offers, and the campaign goes after Google and Okta sign-ins.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: You accept an invitation to a paid expert interview or webinar, follow the link to a fake Google or Okta sign-in page, and the attacker reuses the login against your SSO-protected cloud and GitHub access.
lockItDown: In your Google Account under Security, review 'Your devices' and recent security activity for sign-ins you do not recognise; do the same for recent activity in your Okta account.
Check that your Google and Okta sign-in policies require a phishing-resistant factor (passkey or FIDO2 security key) rather than codes or push.
incidents.roleAngle: Paid expert-interview offers are a believable lure for senior technical staff; flag this to colleagues who take expert-network calls.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Microsoft Store App Found Delivering Vinci RAT Capable of Remote System Control

incidents.title: Microsoft Store app and fake snipping-tool site used to deliver Vinci RAT on Windows
incidents.evidenceQuote: begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool
incidents.tldrRootCause: Victims were redirected to a fake snipping-tool site that served a Microsoft-signed installer leading to Vinci RAT.
incidents.realisticRootCause: According to eSentire as cited in the teaser, the intrusion starts with a redirect to a bogus snipping-tool site that provides a Microsoft-signed installer named Snipping-Tool.exe, and a Microsoft Store application delivers the RAT. The excerpt is cut off before the remaining steps.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes on Windows laptops, if someone installs a screenshot or snipping utility from a look-alike site or an unfamiliar Store listing.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A Windows user searching for a snipping tool could land on the fake site and run the signed installer, giving an attacker remote control of a laptop that holds cloud and GitHub sessions.
lockItDown: On Windows laptops, open Settings > Apps > Installed apps and check for snipping or screenshot tools whose publisher is not Microsoft or that nobody remembers installing.
Check the Downloads folder and EDR or Defender history for a file named Snipping-Tool.exe obtained from a website instead of being built into Windows.
incidents.roleAngle: A Microsoft signature and Store delivery did not make this installer safe, so signing alone should not be treated as an allow-list criterion.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions

incidents.title: binary-parser library before 2.3.1 allows code injection via parser definitions
incidents.evidenceQuote: could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code
incidents.tldrRootCause: A code injection flaw in binary-parser lets someone who controls parser definitions run arbitrary code; no exploitation is reported.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS 9.2 / 8.1) is a code injection bug affecting binary-parser versions before 2.3.1. It is exploitable when an attacker can influence the parser definitions the library is given.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if a project of yours depends on binary-parser below 2.3.1 and builds parser definitions from untrusted input.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A service or tool in your GitHub repositories that pulls in binary-parser, directly or transitively, and builds parser definitions from external data could be made to run attacker-supplied JavaScript.
lockItDown: Search your repositories' lockfiles and GitHub Dependabot alerts for binary-parser and confirm that it resolves to 2.3.1 or later.
Where it is used, check whether parser definitions (field names, lengths, options) are ever derived from user or external input instead of being hardcoded.
incidents.roleAngle: The severity depends on attacker control of parser definitions, so triage by how the library is used and not by the CVSS score alone.
